title: Chapter 13
paragraphs: When they rose from the table, Levin would have liked to follow Kitty into the drawing room, but he was afraid she might dislike it as too obvious a show of attention. He stayed in the little knot of men, taking part in the general conversation, and without looking at Kitty he was aware of her movements, her looks, and where she was in the room.

He kept, at once and without the slightest effort, the promise he had made her — always to think well of all men and to like everyone always. The talk turned to the village commune, which Pestsov regarded as a sort of special principle, calling it the "choral" principle. Levin did not agree with Pestsov, nor with his brother, who had his own attitude — at once admitting and not admitting the significance of the Russian commune. But he talked with them, only trying to reconcile and soften their differences. He had no interest in what he was saying himself, and even less in what they were saying; all he wanted was for them, and for everyone, to be happy and content. He now knew the one thing of importance; and that one thing was first there, in the drawing room, and then began moving across the rooms until it came to a stop at the door. Without turning round he could feel the eyes fixed on him, and the smile, and he could not help turning. She was standing in the doorway with Shtcherbatsky, looking at him.
"I thought you were heading for the piano," he said, going over to her. "That's something I miss in the country — music."
"No; we only came to fetch you and thank you," she said, rewarding him with a smile that was like a gift, "for coming. What do they want to argue about? No one ever convinces anyone, you know."
"Yes, that's true," Levin said; "it generally happens that one argues warmly simply because one can't make out what one's opponent is trying to prove."

Levin had often noticed in discussions between the most intelligent people that after enormous effort, and an enormous expenditure of logical subtleties and words, the disputants finally realized that what they had been struggling so long to prove to each other had been known to both of them from the beginning, but that they liked different things and would not say what they liked for fear it would be attacked. He had often experienced suddenly, in the middle of an argument, grasping what it was his opponent liked and at once liking it himself, and immediately finding himself in agreement, after which all the arguments fell away as useless. Sometimes he had had the opposite experience: he had finally come out with what he himself liked, which he had been devising arguments to defend, and, by chance hitting on a happy and sincere phrase for it, had found his opponent agreeing on the spot and dropping the dispute. He tried to say this.
She furrowed her brow, trying to follow him. But the moment he began to illustrate the point with an example, she understood at once.
"I see: one has to find out what he is arguing for, what is precious to him, then one can...."

She had grasped completely and put into words his clumsily expressed idea. Levin smiled joyfully; he was struck by the leap from the muddled, wordy debate with Pestsov and his brother to this brief, clear, almost wordless communication of the most complex ideas.
Shtcherbatsky moved away from them, and Kitty, walking over to a card table, sat down, picked up the chalk, and began drawing diverging circles on the new green cloth.

They went back to the subject that had been raised at dinner — the freedom and occupations of women. Levin agreed with Darya Alexandrovna that a girl who did not marry should find a woman's duties within a family. He supported this by pointing out that no family can manage without women's help; that in every family, poor or rich, there must be nurses, either relatives or hired.
"No," Kitty said, blushing but looking at him all the more boldly with her truthful eyes; "a girl may be so placed that she can't live in the family without humiliation, while she herself...."
He caught her meaning at once.
"Oh, yes," he said. "Yes, yes, yes — you're right; you're right!"

And he saw all that Pestsov had been arguing at dinner about the freedom of women, simply from a glimpse of the terror of an old maid's life and its humiliation in Kitty's heart; and loving her, he felt that terror and humiliation, and at once gave up his arguments.

A silence fell. She was still drawing with the chalk on the table. Her eyes were shining with a soft light. Under the spell of her mood he felt in his whole being a steadily growing tension of happiness.
"Ah! I've scribbled all over the table!" she said, and laying down the chalk, made a movement as if to get up.

"What! Am I to be left alone — without her?" he thought in horror, and he picked up the chalk. "Wait a minute," he said, sitting down at the table. "There's something I've been wanting to ask you for a long time."
He looked straight into her caressing, though frightened, eyes.
"Please, ask it."

"Here," he said; and he wrote the initial letters, _w, y, t, m, i, c, n, b, d, t, m, n, o, t_. These letters meant: "When you told me it could never be, did that mean never, or then?" There seemed no likelihood that she could make out this complicated sentence; but he looked at her as though his life depended on her understanding it. She glanced at him seriously, then leaned her puckered brow on her hands and began to read. Once or twice she stole a glance at him, as if asking, "Is it what I think?"
"I understand," she said, flushing slightly.
"What is this word?" he said, pointing to the _n_ that stood for _never_.
"It means _never_," she said; "but that's not true!"
He quickly rubbed out what he had written, handed her the chalk, and stood up. She wrote, _t, i, c, n, a, d_.

Dolly was entirely comforted from the depression caused by her talk with Alexey Alexandrovitch when she caught sight of the two figures: Kitty with the chalk in her hand, looking up at Levin with a shy and happy smile, and his handsome figure bending over the table, his glowing eyes one moment on the table and the next on her. Suddenly he was radiant: he had understood. It meant, "Then I could not have answered differently."
He glanced at her questioningly, timidly.
"Only then?"
"Yes," her smile answered.
"And n... and now?" he asked.
"Well, read this. I'll tell you what I would like — would like so much!" She wrote the initial letters, _i, y, c, f, a, f, w, h._ This meant, "If you could forget and forgive what happened."
He snatched up the chalk with nervous, trembling fingers, breaking it, and wrote the initial letters of the following: "I have nothing to forget and to forgive; I have never ceased to love you."
She glanced at him with a smile that did not waver.
"I understand," she said in a whisper.
He sat down and wrote a long phrase. She understood it all and, without asking "Is it this?" took the chalk and answered at once.

For a long while he could not make out what she had written, and kept looking into her eyes. He was stupefied with happiness. He could not supply the word she had meant; but in her charming eyes, beaming with happiness, he saw everything he needed to know. And he wrote three letters. But he had barely finished writing when she read them over his arm, and herself finished and wrote the answer: "Yes."
"Playing _secrétaire_?" said the old prince. "But we really must be off if you want to be in time for the theater."
Levin got up and walked Kitty to the door.
In their conversation everything had been said; it had been said that she loved him, and that she would tell her father and mother that he would come tomorrow morning.
